summary: @rixxcodex/baileys fetches attacker-controlled IDs at runtime and drives authenticated WhatsApp actions on the installer's account
details: This fork of Baileys wires two covert remote-control channels into the socket setup. In lib/Socket/socket.js, makeSocket's validateConnection calls a helper that reconstructs the URL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skyzopedia/NewsletterID/refs/heads/main/VIP_Push.js from a char-code array, fetches a JSON list, and after a delay dispatches authenticated `iq w:mex` queries whose newsletter_id values come from that remote list — letting the repository owner push arbitrary WhatsApp control actions through the installer's authenticated session. In the newsletter module, loadBase base64-decodes https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skyzopedia/Screaper/refs/heads/main/idChannel.json, fetches the id list, and invokes newsletterWMexQuery(id, FOLLOW) for each entry, silently subscribing the installer's account to attacker-chosen newsletter channels. A separate generateMessageV builds a WhatsApp @newsletter JID by XOR-decoding a base64 literal with key 23 and dispatches it via a 40-second setTimeout with a hardcoded query id, matching the same covert-action machinery. The package also declares its core crypto dependency as `"@rixxcodex/libsignal": "github:RixxCode/libsignal"` with no commit SHA or tag, so npm install pulls whatever the default branch currently points at and executes it on every load. The mutable third-party URLs, char-code and base64/XOR concealment of the destinations, delayed dispatch, and use of the installer's authenticated WhatsApp session to perform actions the caller never requested are not part of the advertised Baileys API.

cwes.description: The product contains code that appears to be malicious in nature.
